An asset that travels with the worker#

For a junior engineer deciding whether to pay for instruction, qualification has value because it opens a stream of expert earnings that remains available after changing employers. We measure that value by Δ\DeltaΔ, the difference between discounted lifetime income as an expert and as a novice, so borrowing against future earnings connects today’s tuition to tomorrow’s professional opportunities.

Formal study produces a qualification intensity xxx, with a resource cost κx2/2\kappa x^2/2κx2/2 that becomes steeper as study intensifies, while qualification becomes obsolete at rate δ\deltaδ. Choosing study balances its marginal expense against its expected capital gain, giving x=Δ/κx=\Delta/\kappax=Δ/κ, through which a higher qualification value raises the rate at which each novice invests.

Diagnostic placements provide a second source of entry, and complete pricing transfers the placement’s private capital gain to its seller through the apprenticeship payment. After that payment is accounted for, practice still changes the population acquiring qualification, while future wage premia determine the private value that guides formal study, a division derived from the worker’s value equations on pages 16–18.

Why replacement is incomplete#

Within the stationary comparison, we hold the expert-demand schedule fixed and remove diagnostic content from a purchased portfolio whose service requirements remain unchanged. At the old expert population, fewer practice transitions leave entry below the flow needed to replace obsolescence, so the stationary population moves downward until formal entry and the remaining diagnostic entry once again balance qualification loss.

As experts become scarcer, a decreasing inverse demand schedule raises their hourly wage, which raises the qualification value and each novice’s study intensity. At the same time, the smaller expert share leaves more novices able to undertake study, so aggregate formal transitions increase through both the number of learners and, where wages respond strictly, their individual investment.

Full replacement would preserve the old population and its old wage, which would also preserve the old private incentive to study, whereas the increased investment in this comparison is supported by changed career returns. Flow balance then gives a sharper statement, because the lost practice equals the increase in formal transitions plus the reduction in replacement needs caused by the smaller expert population.

For any finite practice reduction inside the feasible stationary interval, formal transitions rise by a strictly positive amount smaller than the lost practice, and total teaching resources also rise. Proposition C.1 obtains that finite comparison from monotonicity, including continuous demand schedules with corners, while the differentiable formula in the mathematical chapter measures the fraction replaced locally.

Higher hourly earnings and fewer recipients#

When the expert population falls, the remaining experts receive higher hourly earnings wherever demand slopes strictly downward, and their qualification becomes a more valuable private asset. Total income received by the occupation also counts how many experts remain, so its response combines the wage increase with the reduction in people receiving that wage.

Within the service-and-training economy, isoelastic expert demand DS=Cw−εD_S=Cw^{-\varepsilon}DS​=Cw−ε and clearing E=DSE=D_SE=DS​ give total expert income proportional to E1−1/εE^{1-1/\varepsilon}E1−1/ε, producing a fall in the wage bill after practice loss when ε>1\varepsilon>1ε>1. Within that region, someone observing higher professional rates and someone observing lower total expert income would be measuring distinct outcomes of the same stationary adjustment.

Novice finances require their own account because placement payments and tuition reduce current cash income while purchased training changes future earnings. Lifetime values incorporate those investments, and the benchmark’s stationary novice value is b/ρ+Δ2/(2κρ)b/\rho+\Delta^2/(2\kappa\rho)b/ρ+Δ2/(2κρ), where bbb is the basic outside wage and ρ\rhoρ is the discount rate, making explicit the difference between current receipts and the value of a career.

When customer discovery also expands service demand, the demand shift raises training incentives even at a fixed expert population, introducing a second source of entry alongside the scarcity response. Expertise falls in that comparison when the diagnostic loss exceeds the formal entry induced by the direct demand shift, so the separate effects on practice and purchased expert hours retain their economic role.

Future opportunities enter present study#

During a transition, the professional population is inherited from earlier learning and obsolescence, while qualification value responds to the future wages that a newly qualified person expects to receive. Announcements about future customer demand or research automation can change that value immediately, which allows current study to move before the announced technology changes current work.

With the same terminal career payoff, the difference in present qualification values equals a positively weighted integral of the two future wage paths, giving a direct connection between anticipated earnings and current investment. Once research competes for the same people, its method choices become part of those expected wages, and the shared research market supplies the next part of the argument.

Within the interactive career figure, both paths begin with expert share E(0)=0.55E(0)=0.55E(0)=0.55 and frontier A(0)=1A(0)=1A(0)=1, and the finite career payoff is Δ(T)=0\Delta(T)=0Δ(T)=0, so formal study approaches zero at the terminal date as the remaining investment horizon closes. Those paths solve the evolving joint economy, while the stationary replacement result above compares fixed-frontier equilibria whose qualification values remain positive.

Numerical quantities use the model’s normalized units and the selected economy’s demand, practice, and research parameters, with the comparison curve retaining the human-research baseline. Selecting the announcement case includes changes in method availability and can cross research regimes, while the signed anticipation theorem in the next chapter follows a comparison in which both economies remain mixed.
